title: Mutational scanning reveals substrate-assisted autoregulation of the WNT destruction complex.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed the processed screen tables from the authors' GitHub/Zenodo code deposit: dc_abe_for_z_score_plots.xlsx (4,897 rows x 17 cols), dc_cbe_for_zscore_plots.xlsx (5,271 x 17), dc_cbe_wnt_raw_countsavg_LFC.xlsx (5,395 x 14, two replicates per sorted bin), dc_cbe_aa_3_10_distinct.xlsx (6,549 guide-to-predicted-mutation annotations). Confirmed: guide sequence present, z-scores for the top and bottom reporter bins present with zero missing values, 0 duplicate guide sequences, 279/278 non-targeting control guides, 1-9 predicted amino-acid changes per guide, replicate read-count correlation r = 0.96-0.98 (log scale), and a working positive control (CTNNB1 degron residues 30-50 mean top-bin z = 2.05 versus -0.22 for the rest of CTNNB1).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The claim of ~150 previously unreported signalling-altering mutations, the identity of the reporter cell line and sorting gates, and the biological conclusions about the AXIN1-beta-catenin interface. Nature's own supplementary tables could not be retrieved (Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out), so the paper's stated library sizes were not cross-checked against the files. Raw sequencing is in NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA1344315 and was deliberately not downloaded.

a1_downloadable.note: Processed tables download anonymously from the authors' GitHub repository and its Zenodo archive; no login. Verified by downloading four files.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: At the guide level the label is already a column (z_score_top, z_score_bot, plus B_U_lFC/T_U_lFC log fold changes). Caveat verified in the files: a per-amino-acid-variant label is NOT a column, because only 1,206 of 4,897 adenine-base-editor guides and 1,555 of 5,271 cytosine-base-editor guides have a single predicted mutation; the rest would need deconvolution.

a3_inputs_present.note: 20-nt guide sequence, gene symbol, residue number and predicted amino-acid substitutions are all in the table; protein sequences for the four genes come from UniProt with four lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Columns are reads per million, log-normalized counts, log fold change versus unsorted, and z-scores standardized to non-targeting controls; non-targeting mean z is exactly 0.000 in both files, confirming the normalization.

a5_enough_rows.note: 4,897 adenine-base-editor + 5,271 cytosine-base-editor guides = 10,168 labelled rows (counted). Only 1,401 of these are single-mutation missense guides, which is below the ~1,500 threshold if you insist on clean variant-level labels.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3 MB of spreadsheets plus four protein sequences
a6_fits_laptop.note: Entire processed dataset is under 5 MB; verified by downloading it.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Row counts are internally consistent (5,395 raw cytosine-editor rows filter to 5,271 scored rows). Paper-side library sizes could not be checked because the supplementary tables were not retrievable, so this is a partial pass.

a8_label_provenance.note: Label is a physical measurement: cells sorted by a WNT fluorescent reporter, guides counted by sequencing, z-scored against non-targeting guides. Not a model output. Important caveat: the mutation annotation used as a FEATURE is predicted by the authors' base-editor design tool, not genotyped, so feature noise (not label circularity) is the risk.

B1.why: Two screen tables with identical 17-column schemas, trivially concatenable; annotation tables join on guide sequence.

B2.why: Excel files, not csv/parquet, but parsed first try with pandas/openpyxl, no header mangling.

B3.why: Z-scores already normalized to non-targeting controls by authors, but adenine and cytosine screens normalized separately.

B4.why: Zero missing z-scores; only control rows lack mutation annotation. No censored values in files.

B5.why: Verified 0 duplicated guide sequences within each of the two screen tables.

B6.why: Column names self-explanatory and an R pipeline is provided, but no data dictionary; mutation_category semantics inferred.

C1.why: Transfer question is informative, but with weak per-guide signal a null result could just be assay noise.

C2.why: ESM-2 and ProteinGym give open, honestly benchmarked variant-effect predictors; BE-Hive/DeepBE open for editing outcomes; none on this readout.

C3.why: Unique-application angle (base-editor screen scores as a protein language model target) but only four genes, one pathway.

C4.why: Base-editor screens with fluorescence sorting and sequencing are months of wet-lab work per gene.

C5.why: ESM-2 zero-shot and a mutation-class/position dummy are obvious baselines; no published number on this dataset.

D1.why: ESM-2 protein language model has open downloadable weights and the data are four human proteins.

D2.why: Only four sequences to embed, so embeddings cache in minutes on CPU; APC at 2,843 residues needs windowing.

D3.why: ESM-2 weights are MIT-licensed; the screen data sit in a GitHub repo with a permissive LICENSE file.

E1.why: Can hold out whole genes, or contiguous residue blocks/domains, to prevent neighbouring-guide leakage.

E2.why: Only four target genes; domain-level groups exist but gene-level holdout gives fewer than five groups.

E3.why: Per-gene mean and per-mutation-class mean are computable directly from the table.

E4.why: Verified two replicates per sorted bin (read-count r = 0.96-0.98) and silent/non-targeting guide spread gives a noise floor.

E5.why: Verified in files: CTNNB1 degron residues 30-50 mean top-bin z = 2.05 vs -0.22 elsewhere; CTNNB1 nonsense guides lose signalling.

E6.why: Label shuffling and feature-block ablation (guide sequence vs mutation annotation vs position) are one-liners.

E7.why: A separate Nature Genetics saturation-editing study of all 342 CTNNB1 degron missense variants (PMC12900645) gives an independent second measurement.

E8.why: No published machine-learning number exists on this dataset to reproduce.

G1.why: Gene symbols and residue numbers present, but UniProt accession and isoform numbering must be resolved (only four lookups).

G2.why: Named partners: the CTNNB1 saturation-editing dataset, MaveDB/ProteinGym, and AlphaFold DB / PDB destruction-complex structures.

G3.why: Guide-to-mutation is one-to-many (up to 9 predicted changes per guide); a collapse rule must be decided first.

G4.why: Combined question (does structural interface context explain signalling effect better than sequence alone?) is real but modest in scope.

H1.why: Silent (564/498), intron and non-targeting (279/278) controls present, and effects measured in both reporter directions.

H2.why: One lab, one reporter cell line, four genes, one pathway; verified from gene_names column.

H3.why: The honest claim can be stated precisely in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: Paper discusses base-editing coverage limits, but bystander-edit ambiguity is only visible once you count mutations per guide.

I1.why: Rohatgi lab (Stanford), Gerlach/Cook groups and WNT-inhibitor developers such as StemSynergy are named stakeholders.

I2.why: Could prioritize which AXIN1-beta-catenin interface mutations to test next, but the paper already names its top hits.

I3.why: Users need a ranked shortlist of hits; regression on z-score is roughly aligned but not the decision itself.

I4.why: A lookup by mutation class plus residue position likely captures much of the signal; machine learning helps somewhat.

J1.why: Involves grouped splits, protein language model transfer, honest negative controls - the skills worth learning.

J2.why: WNT destruction-complex biology is readable from the paper, but judging individual predictions needs an expert check.

J3.why: A cleaned, deconvolved variant-level table of 10,168 guides is a shareable artefact even if the model is mediocre.

J4.why: Scope is small (days) but no time budget was committed.

J5.why: No kill date written anywhere yet.

existing_models.name: ESM-2 (protein language model, Meta)
existing_models.score_and_split: Zero-shot benchmarked across 217 deep mutational scanning assays in ProteinGym; typical Spearman correlation roughly 0.4 averaged over assays, random-variant splits
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Zero-shot scores are poor for assays where fitness is a cellular signalling readout rather than stability or binding, and for mutations in disordered regions

existing_models.name: ProteinGym benchmark suite
existing_models.score_and_split: Provides leaderboard scores for ~80 predictors on random, modulo and contiguous-position splits
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalization to new proteins and to multi-mutant and indel variants

existing_models.name: BE-Hive (base-editing outcome predictor, Broad)
existing_models.score_and_split: Predicts base-editing efficiency and bystander genotype outcomes from target sequence; reported Pearson correlations around 0.7-0.9 on held-out target libraries
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Bystander-edit uncertainty and transfer across editor variants and cell types

existing_models.name: DeepBE (deep learning, 63 base editors)
existing_models.score_and_split: Editing efficiency/outcome prediction across 63 editor-Cas9 combinations, held-out target sequences

existing_models.name: Base-editor sgRNA fitness-score model (Orro et al., preprint)
existing_models.score_and_split: Classifies depleting base-editor guides in proliferation screens, AUC-ROC above 0.93 across cell lines; split described as held-out guides within cell lines
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Predictions are driven by guide sequence rather than editing efficiency, so the mutation-level biology is not captured

backbone.name: ESM-2 (esm2_t12_35M or t33_650M), with windowing for APC's 2,843 residues
backbone.hardware: CPU laptop; only four protein sequences to embed

integration.partner_dataset: The companion Nature Genetics CTNNB1 degron saturation-editing dataset (all 342 missense variants, PMC12900645) plus AlphaFold DB / PDB structures of the destruction complex
integration.join_key: UniProt accession plus residue number (CTNNB1 P35222, APC P25054, AXIN1 O15169, GSK3B P49841)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do base-editor screen scores, which average over bystander edits, recover the same per-variant signalling effects as saturation genome editing, and does adding structural interface distance explain the residual?

controls.positive_control: Verified in the files: CTNNB1 degron residues 30-50 are strongly enriched in the high-WNT bin (mean z = 2.05 adenine editor, 1.39 cytosine editor, versus -0.22 and -0.84 for the rest of CTNNB1), and CTNNB1 nonsense guides lose signalling (bottom-bin z = 2.30).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle z-scores within gene and confirm collapse to the per-gene mean; ablate the mutation-annotation feature block and keep only raw guide sequence.
controls.external_validation: The independent CTNNB1 saturation-editing dataset covering all 342 degron missense variants; also train on the cytosine-editor screen and test on the adenine-editor screen.

honest_claim_h3: From a guide RNA's predicted amino-acid changes and a protein language model embedding, we can rank base-editing guides by their effect on a WNT fluorescent reporter in one engineered cell line, across four destruction-complex genes only, with per-variant resolution limited by bystander edits.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use protein sequence context of base-edited positions to predict how strongly each edit changes WNT signalling output.
plain_idea.train_on: 10,168 CRISPR base-editing guide RNAs (4,897 adenine-editor, 5,271 cytosine-editor, counted in the files), each with its 20-nucleotide guide sequence, target gene, residue number and 1-9 predicted amino-acid substitutions in CTNNB1, APC, AXIN1 or GSK3B.
plain_idea.predict: A continuous enrichment z-score for how much the edit pushes cells into the high- or low-WNT-reporter bin. The truth comes from sorting reporter cells by fluorescence and counting guides by sequencing, normalized to non-targeting guides.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: WNT drug-discovery groups want to know which destruction-complex interface mutations strengthen or break the complex; a model that ranks them would tell them which mutations to make next without running another screen.

pitch.headline: 10,168 base-editing guides with WNT-reporter enrichment z-scores, 557 control guides, and a positive control I confirmed works in the files.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Two orthogonal base editors scanned the same four destruction-complex genes in the same reporter line, so the cytosine screen can externally validate the adenine screen - rare in mutational-scanning data.
pitch.the_win: Beat ESM-2's zero-shot correlation on held-out residue blocks, and show base-editor z-scores agree with the independent CTNNB1 saturation-editing scores at the same positions.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: You learn how much bystander-edit averaging destroys per-variant signal in base-editor screens - a number nobody has published and that anyone reusing such screens needs.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Rohatgi lab (Stanford) and WNT-inhibitor developers deciding which AXIN1-beta-catenin interface residues to mutate next; also anyone mining base-editor screens as mutational-scanning data.

ml_idea: Concatenate the adenine- and cytosine-editor tables, attach ESM-2 embeddings of the edited residue window for each predicted substitution, aggregate over the 1-9 predicted mutations per guide, and regress the reporter z-score with a ridge/gradient-boosting head. Evaluate with contiguous-residue-block and held-out-gene splits, with a mutation-class plus position dummy and ESM-2 zero-shot as baselines; validate CTNNB1 predictions against the independent saturation-editing dataset.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: four protein sequences to embed with ESM-2 on CPU (APC in sliding windows) takes minutes; the model table is ~10k rows so cross-validation is seconds to minutes. Files were downloaded and parsed, so sizes are measured.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count how many guides have exactly one predicted amino-acid change AND a well-separated z-score: I already counted 1,401 single-mutation missense guides, below the 1,500-row comfort threshold - next check whether the silent-guide z-score spread swallows most missense effects (silent mean z differs from missense by under 0.1 in both screens).

verdict_reason: Clean, small, fully downloadable data with a real measured label and a positive control I verified in the files, but the scope is narrow (four genes, one reporter cell line, one lab) and the label is per-guide averaged over up to nine bystander edits, so only 1,401 guides give clean single-variant labels. With only four genes there are too few groups for a convincing held-out-protein split, and open zero-shot variant-effect predictors are already honestly benchmarked. Worth parking as a short transfer/agreement study against the independent CTNNB1 saturation-editing dataset rather than a main project.
